idiom_name: std::async + std::future/std::promise (blocking get() as the only wait)
implementation_notes: std::async(std::launch::async, f) starts the work immediately and returns a std::future that will hold the result: the start-now half of the pattern with a value handle for later. std::future has no continuation, so 'later' is either a blocking get() at the point of use or a std::promise completed elsewhere and observed by whoever holds the future; pass std::launch::async explicitly so the implementation cannot silently defer the call until get(). This is the default realization when no framework is available; reach for a handler-based library or coroutines when the caller must not block at all.
pitfalls: A future with no continuation turns 'result later' into a blocking get(); calling that on the thread which must deliver the completion is the C++ form of sync-over-async.
An unconsumed future blocks in the destructor of its shared state (std::async's future waits), so dropping the handle can stall the caller silently.
Without std::launch::async the implementation may defer the call until get()/wait(), which removes the start-now property entirely.

variants.name: Boost.Asio async operation + completion handler on the io_context
variants.idiom_name: Boost.Asio async_* + completion handler driven by io_context.run()
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Asio implements the explicit event form: an initiating function such as async_read_some returns immediately and stores the caller's handler, and io_context.run() invokes that handler later - on the loop thread, not in the initiating call - delivering the error_code and the transferred size ('a consistent asynchronous model using a modern C++ approach'). Handlers own their captured state, so per-call data must be moved into them; compose chains with lambdas/bind or the newer use_awaitable/use_future completion tokens.
pitfalls: Handlers and everything they capture must live until the operation completes; capturing a stack frame that has returned is Asio's classic use-after-free.
Never block inside a completion handler: a single-threaded io_context runs one handler at a time, so blocking there stalls every other pending completion - post heavy work to another executor.

variants.name: C++20 coroutine (co_await) over the same completion mechanism
variants.idiom_name: co_await on an awaitable; coroutine_handle::resume is the completion
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 coroutines linearise the handler chains: co_await suspends the coroutine and the operation's completion resumes it, so the call still completes asynchronously but reads sequentially. The machinery is unchanged - a completion callback lives in the coroutine frame and resumes the handle - so this is the same pattern with better ergonomics; use it where the toolchain is C++20 and long callback chains hurt readability, and see C++26 execution senders/receivers whose completion functions are set_value/set_error/set_stopped.
pitfalls: The coroutine frame owns the state: a coroutine that outlives the objects it references (or whose promise/allocator is wrong) resumes into freed memory.
co_await works only on awaitables; wrapping a raw callback API still needs an adapter that resumes the handle exactly once - resuming twice or never is undefined behaviour or a hang.
